subject: Analyzing copy number in cancer samples

messages.author: 339f24fca4be8308
messages.subject: Analyzing copy number in cancer samples
parts:
Hi, I am processing a great number of cancer samples using the Hapmap
samples as reference. In the command,

plm.as <- AvgCnPlm(csC, ...)

is it possible to use previously estimated probe affinities ( e.g.
from the reference set ) to process the test set? I get the cancer
samples a few at a time and so don't want to re-estimate the probe
affinities every time a new cancer sample is fit.

Thanks! -Nancy

messages.author: 185f4d4fdb048fb8
messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Analyzing copy number in cancer samples
parts:
On Feb 19, 2008 11:34 PM, Nancy <nrz...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi, I am processing a great number of cancer samples using the Hapmap
> samples as reference. In the command,
>
> plm.as <- AvgCnPlm(csC, ...)
>
> is it possible to use previously estimated probe affinities ( e.g.
> from the reference set ) to process the test set? I get the cancer
> samples a few at a time and so don't want to re-estimate the probe
> affinities every time a new cancer sample is fit.

Did you mean RmaCnPlm(), because all AvgCnPlm() is doing is estimating
the robust average across all probe intensities. In the chip
effect/probe affinities worlds this corresponds to fixing all probe
affinities to one.

So, first for the RmaCnPlm, unfortunately you cannot reuse the probe
affinities. This idea has been raised many times, especially for
large data sets. It has been on the todo list almost from the very
beginning, but it never makes it up to the top before something else
pushes it down.

Back to the AvgCnPlm. This is not really a two-way model with chip
effects and probe affinities because the latter are all ones. A
two-way model is a multi-array model, whereas the AvgCnPlm model is a
single-array model. However, due to lack of time, I utilized the
RmaCnPlm framework to implement AvgCnPlm, which means that in practice
"fits" the model across array (probeset by probeset). Thus, the real
solution will be to reimplement AvgCnPlm to do the "fit" for each
array separately. Which would solve your problem. [Thus, with
allelic crosstalk calibration and an updated summarization
implementation, the method is truly single-array up to that point].
...on my todo list.

It is also on my todo list to speed up the processing by identifying
all single-probe unit groups and simple "fit" those by taking the chip
effect as the probe intensity. For the GWS5/GWS6 that would speed up
things quite a bit since half of the units are CN probes.

/Henrik

>
> Thanks! -Nancy
> >

Hi Henrik,

Thanks, this is helpful. I am trying everything on the 100K first and
then planning to move to 6.0, so you are right, it should be RmaCnPlm.

One more question: I want to use RmaCnPlm to analyze some cancer
samples, but if the batch contain *only* cancer samples, would the
probe level estimates in copy number variant regions be wrong?

So I tried grouping the cancer samples with some normal samples to be
analyzed together. But the cancer samples use the Early Access 100K
array, while the normal samples are the regular 100K array. Can these
two be analyzed together? Or, maybe I'm wrong and don't need to worry
about this...

Nancy

messages.author: 185f4d4fdb048fb8
messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Re: Analyzing copy number in cancer samples
parts:
On Thu, Feb 21, 2008 at 11:33 AM, Nancy <nrz...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Henrik,
>
> Thanks, this is helpful. I am trying everything on the 100K first and
> then planning to move to 6.0, so you are right, it should be RmaCnPlm.
>
> One more question: I want to use RmaCnPlm to analyze some cancer
> samples, but if the batch contain *only* cancer samples, would the
> probe level estimates in copy number variant regions be wrong?

Your chip-effect estimates will be standardized towards the robust
average of all arrays. That's is basically true for all probe-level
summarization models. In other words, your chip effects will be
relative to the average cancer sample.

>
> So I tried grouping the cancer samples with some normal samples to be
> analyzed together. But the cancer samples use the Early Access 100K
> array, while the normal samples are the regular 100K array. Can these
> two be analyzed together? Or, maybe I'm wrong and don't need to worry
> about this...

No, unfortunately you cannot mix two different chip types in
probe-level summarization.

The only way I can see how this could be done is to identify all
probes that are in common in the two chip types and only work with
those, and ignore all other probes in the summarization step. In
order to do this, you will need to create a custom CDF for this
"joint" chip type, and then transform all CEL files to map to this new
CDF by reshuffling the probes. To minimize the amount of work for
this, the probe indices in custom CDF can be chosen to map to the main
chip type (say Mapping50K_Hind240) and then you only have to reshuffle
the CEL files for the Early Access version. All bits and pieces for
doing this is available in aroma.affymetrix and affxparser, but in
order to do it, you have to know quite a bit about how CEL and CDF
files work.

Another alternative is fit the 100K cancer samples and the EA100K
normal samples separately (if you got enough of them), and combine
them on the chip-effect level. Say 'ces' and 'cesEA' are
CnChipEffectSet estimates for the 100K and the EA100K chip type. Then
you can extract chip effects as:

data <- extractDataFrame(ces, addNames=TRUE)
dataEA <- extractDataFrame(cesEA, addNames=TRUE)

[until next release is available, you have to install patches for this
to work, i.e. downloadPackagePatch("aroma.affymetrix")]

Then you have to match the unit names in the two sets - data$unitName
and dataEA$unitName, and ignore all other units. Next step is to
bring the two sets of estimates to the same scale. The most basic,
and a bit naive approach, is to use quantile normalization to do
this. In aroma.light (sic!), there is a normalizeQuantile() that
takes a matrix (rows are units and columns arrays) and returns a
normalized matrix of the same shape. That could work.

If you want to proceed with aroma.affymetrix segmentation methods, you
then face the problem to get that data back into a format recognized
by the package. This basically bring you back to the custom CDF
problem (not completely, but similarly). Otherwise, you use the
DNAcopy and/pr GLAD package standalone.

Cheers

Henrik
